slides.headline:
The sign says
no children.
slides.subline: Korea's no-kids zones are overwhelmingly cafes — and nobody agrees how many of them there are

slides.label: Of the 114 no-kids zones a civic-group survey could actually find in Korea, 84 were cafes. Restaurants were another 22
slides.note: Source: survey by Political Mamas and four partner groups, fieldwork September–December 2025, published January 2026 · via Kyunghyang Shinmun, 6 May 2026 · Checked 21 October 2026

slides.title:
Nobody actually
keeps the count.
slides.body:
You will read that Korea has more than 500 no-kids zones. That figure traces back to a 2023 map anyone could edit, which the Korea Herald put at 451 restaurants and cafes. The civic groups who went looking in late 2025 verified 114. Their live map read 122 on 5 May 2026.

Jeju's own check explains the gap. Of 152 businesses on its list in 2024, only 80 were still turning children away — the rest had dropped the policy or closed. There is no register you can look up. Every number in this post is an estimate, and the honest range is wide.

items.t: No national law bans or permits them
items.d: Refusing entry to children sits in business discretion. There is no statute either way

items.t: The human rights body called it discrimination
items.d: In 2017 the NHRCK found blanket bans on under-13s discriminatory: children's right not to face discrimination outweighs the owner's. The finding is not binding

items.t: The cut-off is whatever the owner picks
items.d: Signs variously bar under-6s, under-10s or under-13s. No age is fixed in law, so it differs shop to shop

items.t: Jeju tried to ban the bans, and failed
items.d: A 2023 ordinance was shelved — no higher law to rest on, and an unfair limit on business freedom. A watered-down awareness ordinance passed instead

items.t: The odds are strongly in your favour
items.d: Even the highest estimate is a few hundred businesses against the 106,452 coffee shops counted nationwide in 2023. A notable practice, not a common one

items.t: Check the listing, don't check the door
items.d: Korean venue pages and reviews flag it. Search the shop's name with 노키즈존, or call and ask: 아이도 들어갈 수 있나요?

items.t: Expect it most in cafes, and on Jeju
items.d: Cafes are three in four of the mapped total. Seoul, Gyeonggi and Jeju hold over 60% between them, and Jeju is far the densest for its size

items.t: There is now a sign for the opposite
items.d: Jeju pays businesses 300,000 won for high chairs and child kit under a Yes Kids Zone scheme — 64 restaurants applied in its first year, 2025

slides.text:
A number that no one
measures will be quoted
as though someone did.
slides.by: Both sides of this argument cite counts that come from volunteers with a shared map. That does not make the practice imaginary — the civic groups verified 114 of them, and Jeju verified 80 in one province alone. It does mean the confident national totals in circulation deserve less weight than they get. This post is research, not a personal visit. Every figure comes from a published source, checked on 21 October 2026.

caption:
You will read that South Korea has more than 500 no-kids zones. It is worth knowing where that number comes from, because it comes from a map anyone could edit. The Korea Herald counted 451 entries on it in 2023. When five civic groups went out and checked, between September and December 2025, they could verify 114 — and their own live map had reached 122 by May 2026. Jeju's provincial government explains the gap neatly: of 152 businesses on its list in 2024, only 80 were still turning children away. The rest had dropped the policy or shut. There is no official register to look up, so treat every figure here, including ours, as an estimate.

What the verified count does show clearly is where the practice lives. Of those 114, 84 were cafes — three in four. Another 22 were restaurants. Seoul, Gyeonggi and Jeju held more than 60% between them.

The legal position surprises people. No national law bans or permits refusing children; it sits in ordinary business discretion. The National Human Rights Commission found in 2017 that blanket bans on under-13s are discriminatory, and that a child's right not to face discrimination outweighs an owner's preference — but that finding carries no legal force. There isn't even a fixed age: signs bar under-6s, under-10s or under-13s depending on who printed them. Jeju tried to outlaw the zones in 2023 and the ordinance was shelved, on the grounds that no higher law authorised it and it would unfairly restrict business freedom. An awareness-raising ordinance passed in its place.

If you're travelling with kids, the practical read is calm. Even the largest estimate is a few hundred businesses against the 106,452 coffee shops counted nationwide in 2023. Check the venue's Korean listing for 노키즈존 before you go rather than finding out at the door, expect it most often in cafes and most densely on Jeju, and note that Jeju now pays businesses 300,000 won for high chairs and child kit to go the other way. Sources in the last slide.
